Laboratory observations of Ferosagitta hispida under controlled conditions have clarified several early life history parameters. At a stable temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], embryonic development proceeds rapidly, with the egg hatching event occurring after 36 hours . The newly emerged larvae measure approximately 0.09 cm  in total length at hatch, a diminutive size that reflects the relatively brief incubation period. Following the chorion rupture, the yolk-sac larva remains lecithotrophic for a short interval before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The duration from fertilization to birth was recorded as 3 days [ab = 3 days] under these same thermal conditions, which is consistent with the rapid developmental pace observed in many chaetognath species at a temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. This swift progression through the earliest stages likely confers a survival advantage by reducing the window of vulnerability to planktonic predators during the most fragile phase of the life cycle. The precise timing of these events is critical for understanding recruitment dynamics in coastal plankton communities.

Growth trajectory analyses for juvenile Ferosagitta hispida indicate that individuals attain morphological and physiological maturity at a relatively modest body size. The total length at puberty, defined by the onset of testis development, reaches 0.76 cm [Lp = 0.76 cm], though field surveys have documented fifty percent puberty occurring across a range from 0.52 cm to 0.68 cm and 0.76 cm based on testis maturation criteria reported by Reeve in 1970. The period from birth to the attainment of this pubertal milestone spans 15 days since birth [tp = 15 days since birth] when measured at 21 °C [T = 21 °C]. Sexual maturation in this species thus represents a notable energetic milestone, as resources must be diverted from somatic growth toward gametogenesis onset. This pubertal length is substantially larger than the hatchling size, indicating a period of pronounced allometric shift during the post-metamorphic juvenile stage. The relatively brief time required to reach reproductive activation suggests that Ferosagitta hispida employs a strategy of rapid development to capitalize on ephemeral planktonic productivity.

The reproductive output of this arrow worm species has been quantified through controlled laboratory rearing experiments. At a constant temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], females produce 68 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 68 eggs per spawning event], with spawning occurring every other day [F_R_i = spawning occurring every other day]. This high fecundity is characteristic of a species that relies on numerical advantage to offset substantial mortality during the planktonic larval phase. The scheduling of these spawning events appears to be tightly coupled with the ingestion of prey items, as the energetic demands of continuous oogenesis are substantial. The ultimate total length attained by fully mature adults reaches 1.2 cm [Li = 1.2 cm], providing the body cavity volume necessary to accommodate the developing oocytes. This size at adulthood represents nearly tenfold the hatchling length and underscores the considerable scope for growth that this species exhibits under optimal feeding conditions.

Feeding ecology plays a central role in supporting the energetic expenditures associated with growth and reproduction in Ferosagitta hispida. Ingestion rates were measured for individuals of 0.85 cm body length, revealing a consumption of 0.64 mg dry weight per day  at an ambient temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This peak food intake rate reflects the high metabolic demands of active hunting in the water column, where these carnivorous chaetognaths pursue copepod prey. The ingestion rate at this body size is substantially higher than that recorded for smaller juveniles, consistent with the scaling of gut volume and hunting appendage size. Temperature exerts a pronounced effect on feeding activity, as the 24 °C condition represents the upper end of the thermal range encountered in their subtropical habitat. Under cooler conditions, metabolic rates decline and ingestion correspondingly decreases, which likely extends the period required to reach the pubertal length threshold.

Longevity records for Ferosagitta hispida indicate that individuals maintained at 21 °C [T = 21 °C] can survive for a maximum of 730 days [am = 730 days], a lifespan that spans approximately two years. This duration is relatively extended for a small planktonic predator and permits multiple reproductive cycles over the lifetime of a single individual. The total length at birth, measuring 0.13 cm [Lb = 0.13 cm], is noticeably larger than the hatchling length of 0.09 cm, reflecting the substantial morphological development achieved during the brief yolk-sac larval stage before the onset of exogenous feeding. The ability to sustain reproductive activity across such a long lifespan depends critically on consistent prey availability and favorable thermal conditions. Senescence in this species likely manifests as a gradual decline in feeding efficiency and egg production rather than a sharp post-reproductive mortality event. Comparative data from related chaetognath species suggest that this lifespan is among the longer recorded for members of the family Sagittidae, highlighting the relatively slow pace of life history in this particular lineage.
